blocks.text: Public or private: which one is right for you?

blocks.html:
Health insurance is compulsory for everyone living in Germany. Without it you cannot get a visa, enrol at a university, start a job or see a doctor.

We help you pick the cover that matches your visa type and your circumstances.

For many newcomers statutory insurance is the natural choice; for others a private plan fits better. Either way, you are insured with an established provider and we handle the paperwork.
The table below compares the two systems, or read our detailed comparison.

items.html: Feature →: Public (statutory) / Private
Who is eligible:: Most applicants, with a few visa types excluded (for example language course visas) / A smaller group; depends on age, health and student status
Are spouse and children covered:: Yes, family members are included / Depends on the plan; family cover is available at extra cost
Which doctors can I see:: Doctors who treat statutory patients / Statutory and private practices
Languages:: Mostly German, some English / English and German with most plans
Accepted visa types:: Bachelor, Master, exchange, employment, internship and more / Bachelor, Master, job seeker, Opportunity Card, language course and more
Monthly cost for students:: Fixed student rate, rises noticeably from age 30 / Fixed student rate, rises moderately from age 30
Monthly cost for employees:: A percentage of income / Depends on age, health and the level of cover
Available in the {{product}}:: Yes / Yes

blocks.html: We work with a small number of insurers that we know serve international customers well: a large statutory health insurer, a digital private health insurer and a specialist for travel and incoming insurance.
If you choose public cover, your membership with our statutory partner starts on the day your studies or your job begin. Statutory insurance is also called public or government health insurance.

Our statutory partner serves a large share of the international students and professionals in Germany. Members benefit from services such as vaccinations, a bonus programme and a digital appointment service.

Students can also choose a private plan from our private insurance partner. Private cover is the alternative to the statutory system and typically includes glasses and contact lenses, dental treatment, a free choice of doctors including private practices, a two-bed hospital room and worldwide cover.

The plan is priced for students and everything, from claims to questions, is handled in the insurer's app.

For the visa and your first weeks in Germany you need a separate type of cover, often called travel health insurance, incoming insurance or Schengen insurance. It is compulsory. Students are covered by it until their studies at a university or university of applied sciences begin.
If you are attending a language course or a preparatory course (Studienkolleg), this private cover runs for the whole duration of the course.
Our partner for this cover is a specialist insurance broker for stays abroad.

blocks.text: How to get health insurance in Germany
Apply online in a few minutes

Take them to your visa appointment as proof of cover. Check the list published by your local consulate, since requirements differ slightly.

After arrival, activate your health insurance in the portal. If you chose the {{product}}, activate your Blocked Account at the same time.

When you need a doctor, book an appointment in the insurer's app at a time that suits you. After the visit, upload the invoice in the app and the reimbursement arrives within a few days.

items.q: Who is eligible for private health insurance?
items.a:
It depends on your situation. Students are frequently eligible.

Book a call with our team or take the insurance quiz to find out.

items.q: Will my university accept the private plan?
items.a:
Yes. German universities are required to accept it.

The plan is a substitutive private health insurance that meets the enrolment requirements under section 193 (3) of the Insurance Contract Act and the long-term care obligation under section 23 (1) of the Social Code, Book XI.

If your university is unsure, tell us. Our insurance team will contact the university and explain the rules.

items.q: Can I switch back to statutory insurance later?
items.a:
A private plan taken out as a student applies for the whole of your studies.

You cannot switch in either direction while you are still enrolled. Once the application is submitted and the university informed, the decision stands.

The one exception: when you turn 30 and the current semester ends, you may move from statutory to private cover to benefit from the lower rate. Students over 30 who stay in the statutory system pay a higher premium because the student rate no longer applies.

After your studies you can switch to statutory insurance. Staying private, or switching to it, requires meeting certain conditions such as a minimum income, self-employment or civil servant status.

In the private system you pay the doctor and the insurer reimburses you. In practice you rarely pay out of pocket:

Most doctors send an invoice with a payment deadline of around four weeks. Upload it in the app and the reimbursement usually arrives before the invoice is due.



For large bills, such as inpatient hospital treatment, the insurer can pay the hospital directly.



Check that a treatment is covered before you go ahead. Some treatments, for example dental implants, require a treatment and cost plan to be approved in advance.

items.q: Can I work while privately insured?
items.a:
Yes.

The plan is a substitutive private insurance and is treated like statutory cover in every official process.

To keep it while working, make sure your contract is a working student contract (Werkstudent) and that you stay under 20 hours a week during the semester. Up to 26 weeks a year you may exceed that limit during semester breaks, evenings or weekends. Going beyond these limits affects your insurance status and your visa.

Tip: if an employer's HR system does not list your insurer, choose "private health insurance". Before accepting a part-time role, confirm that it is a working student contract. If the employer is unsure, our insurance team can explain it to them.


The limits as of 2026:

Up to 20 hours a week: you keep student status and your private cover.

26-week rule: more than 20 hours a week is allowed for up to 26 weeks a year during breaks, evenings or weekends.

Beyond that you lose student status, become an employee and must move to statutory insurance.

Keeping to these limits also keeps you within the conditions of your visa.
The full benefit list is in the plan overview.

items.q: What is the difference between public and private health insurance?
items.a:
Public (statutory, gesetzliche Krankenversicherung)
Run by non-profit insurers under state rules. Premiums depend on your status or income. Cover includes doctor visits, hospital treatment and basic dental care.

Private (private Krankenversicherung)
Run by private companies. Premiums depend on your age, health and the level of cover you choose. Plans often include quicker appointments, private practices and extra benefits.

EC Assets offers both, and both are accepted for visa, enrolment, employment and daily life.

We work only with established insurers.

Read our full comparison of the two systems.

items.q: Is the cover valid for my visa?
items.a:
Yes. Every plan we offer is accepted by the German authorities for visa purposes.

We match the cover to your visa type, so you can apply with confidence.

items.q: What is the difference between travel health insurance and German health insurance?
items.a:
Travel health insurance (incoming insurance) is the cover you show at the visa appointment. It applies to your journey and to the time before your German insurance starts.

After arrival you activate your German health insurance, statutory or private. That cover is compulsory for everyone living in Germany and pays for your everyday medical needs.

items.q: Do I need health insurance in Germany?
items.a:
Yes. German law requires everyone living in the country to be insured.

You must also show travel health insurance at your visa appointment.

All the insurers we work with are recognised by the German authorities.
